 Cat-DPO: Category-Adaptive Safety Alignment

Tiankai Yang ††thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: University of Southern California Email: tiankaiy@usc.edu    Yi Nian* Affiliation: University of Southern California    Xinyuan Li Affiliation: University of Southern California    Ruiyao Xu Affiliation: Northwestern University    Kaize Ding Affiliation: Northwestern University    Yue Zhao Affiliation: University of Southern California
Abstract

Aligning large language models with human preferences must balance two competing goals: responding helpfully to legitimate requests and reliably refusing harmful ones. Most preference-based safety alignment methods collapse safety into a single scalar that is applied uniformly to every preference pair. The result is a model that looks safe on average but stays relatively unsafe on a minority of harm categories. We cast safety alignment as a per-category constrained optimization problem and derive Cat-DPO, a direct-preference-optimization algorithm with a separate adaptive safety margin for each harm category. The margin tightens when the model still produces unsafe responses on a category and relaxes once the model catches up, so the training signal tracks each category’s current difficulty rather than averaging under one global rate. Across two LLM backbones and six preference-learning baselines, Cat-DPO improves aggregate helpfulness and harmlessness and compresses per-category safety variance and the best-to-worst gap, offering a drop-in per-category refinement of direct preference safety alignment.

Warning: This paper contains example data that may be offensive or harmful.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) now underpin general-purpose assistants and are consulted on an ever-widening range of tasks, many of which carry real-world consequences if the model answers badly (Ouyang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026; Nian et al., 2026). Their usefulness in deployment rests on two behaviors that are inherently in tension: responding helpfully to legitimate requests, and reliably refusing or redirecting dangerous, offensive, or illegal ones (Bai et al., 2022; Dai et al., 2024). A model that refuses every request is trivially safe but useless; a model that answers every request is useful but unsafe. Navigating the tension between helpfulness and harmlessness across the full distribution of user inputs is the central challenge of safety alignment.

Most existing methods for safety alignment train on human preference data. Classical RLHF does so in two stages, fitting a reward model on the preferences and then optimizing the policy against that reward model with reinforcement learning (Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022); Safe RLHF (Dai et al., 2024) extends this pipeline with a separate cost model and a PPO-Lagrangian step to enforce a safety constraint. Direct Preference Optimization (Rafailov et al., 2023) later eliminated the reward model by recasting the objective as a classification loss directly on preference pairs, and several safety-focused direct methods, such as SafeDPO (Kim et al., 2026) and SACPO (Wachi et al., 2024), attach a fixed safety signal to the DPO loss. Despite their mechanical differences, these methods all collapse safety into a single scalar, whether a cost budget, a fixed margin, or a soft penalty, applied uniformly to every preference pair regardless of which harm category it touches. A detailed comparison with prior work is deferred to Appendix B.

Uneven performance across subpopulations is a well-documented failure mode of neural networks trained with a single averaged loss (Sagawa* et al., 2020), and the same concern has carried into preference learning, where recent work has explored worst-group and distributionally robust formulations of the DPO objective (Ramesh et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025b; Xu et al., 2025; Chidambaram et al., 2025). Safety alignment is no exception: aggregate safety rates often conceal differences between the best and worst harm categories. Figure 1 illustrates this on PKU-SafeRLHF (Ji et al., 2025): a vanilla DPO baseline reaches a high aggregate harmlessness score but collapses on several low-frequency categories, and even safety-specific direct methods flatten the distribution without closing the residual gaps at the weakest end. The cause is structural: DPO optimizes a single averaged loss, so easy or frequent categories absorb most of the gradient budget while a few persistently unsafe ones receive comparatively little pressure, and the single safety scalar used by Safe RLHF and its direct-alignment successors does not tell the optimization which categories are still lagging.

To address this imbalance, we propose Category-Adaptive Direct Preference Optimization (Cat-DPO), which replaces the single global safety constraint with KK per-category constraints and treats each constraint’s Lagrangian dual variable λk\lambda_{k} as a per-category margin on the DPO loss that is updated online during training. In effect, Cat-DPO replaces the uniform pressure of prior methods with a per-category trajectory tuned to each category’s current difficulty. Experiments across multiple model backbones and safety baselines show that Cat-DPO reduces per-category safety variance and narrows the best-versus-worst gap without sacrificing aggregate safety or helpfulness.

Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We cast safety alignment as a per-category constrained optimization problem and derive the per-category adaptive margin λk\lambda_{k} as the Lagrangian dual variable of the category-kk constraint.

  • •

    We propose Cat-DPO, a practical single-stage training algorithm that realizes the per-category dual updates at the same computational cost as standard DPO.

  • •

    Across multiple backbones and safety baselines, Cat-DPO improves aggregate helpfulness and harmlessness while compressing per-category safety variance and the best-to-worst gap.

2 Preliminaries

We recall the DPO training objective and the single-constraint formulation of safety alignment adopted by Safe RLHF (Dai et al., 2024) and SafeDPO (Kim et al., 2026). These are the two pieces Cat-DPO extends in Section 3.

2.1 DPO and KL-Regularized RL

We work with offline preference data: triples (x,yw,yl)(x,y_{w},y_{l}) in which xx is a prompt and ywy_{w} is preferred to yly_{l} under a binary comparison label. We write (x,yw,yl)∼𝒟(x,y_{w},y_{l})\sim\mathcal{D} for a draw from the empirical preference distribution and assume the labels are consistent with a Bradley–Terry model (Bradley and Terry, 1952) on a latent reward rr, p∗​(yw≻yl∣x)=σ⁡(r⁡(x,yw)−r⁡(x,yl))p^{*}(y_{w}\succ y_{l}\mid x)=\sigma(r(x,y_{w})-r(x,y_{l})), where σ\sigma is the logistic sigmoid.

RLHF optimizes a policy πθ\pi_{\theta} against rr under a KL penalty to a fixed reference model πref\pi_{\text{ref}} (Ziegler et al., 2019),

maxθ𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼πθ(⋅|x)[r(x,y)]−βKL(πθ(⋅|x)∥πref(⋅|x)).\max_{\theta}\;\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\,y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\bigl[r(x,y)\bigr]\;-\;\beta\,\mathrm{KL}\!\bigl(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot|x)\bigr). (1)

The closed-form optimum π∗​(y|x)∝πref​(y|x)​exp⁡(r⁡(x,y)/β)\pi^{*}(y|x)\propto\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)\exp(r(x,y)/\beta) follows from a standard KL-regularized RL argument (Ziegler et al., 2019; Rafailov et al., 2023). Inverting this relation to express rr in terms of π∗/πref\pi^{*}/\pi_{\text{ref}} and substituting back into the Bradley–Terry likelihood eliminates rr entirely, yielding the DPO loss (Rafailov et al., 2023):

ℒDPO​(θ)=−𝔼(x,yw,yl)∼𝒟​[log⁡σ⁡(β​δi)],δi≔log⁡πθ​(yw|x)πref​(yw|x)−log⁡πθ​(yl|x)πref​(yl|x).\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}(\theta)\;=\;-\,\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_{w},y_{l})\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\left[\log\sigma(\beta\delta_{i})\right],\quad\delta_{i}\;\coloneqq\;\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{w}|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{w}|x)}\,-\,\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{l}|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{l}|x)}. (2)

We refer to δi\delta_{i} as the DPO log-ratio throughout.

2.2 Safety Alignment as Constrained Optimization

A common approach to safety alignment augments preference data with a scalar cost signal c⁡(x,y)c(x,y) that is large on harmful responses and non-positive on safe ones, and adds a constraint on this cost to the KL-regularized objective (Dai et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2026). Safe RLHF (Dai et al., 2024) adopts the expected-cost form,

maxθ𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼πθ(⋅|x)[r(x,y)]−βKL(πθ∥πref)s.t.𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼πθ(⋅|x)[c(x,y)]≤d,\max_{\theta}\;\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\,y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}[r(x,y)]-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\,y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}[c(x,y)]\,\leq\,d, (3)

for a scalar budget dd, and solves (3) by PPO-Lagrangian against separately trained reward and cost models. SafeDPO (Kim et al., 2026) instead replaces the expected-cost constraint with the hard condition c⁡(x,y)≤0c(x,y)\leq 0 and recasts the resulting KL-regularized problem as a DPO-style loss on a safety-aware pair-swap of the preference data, with an optional fixed margin Δ≥0\Delta\geq 0. Either way, the safety signal passes through a single scalar that carries no information about which harm category is being violated. This is the structural collapse we revisit in Section 3.

3 Category-Adaptive Direct Preference Optimization

We now derive Cat-DPO. We cast safety alignment as a per-category constrained problem and form its Lagrangian, which yields a category-augmented reward (Section 3.1). Agreement filtering and the DPO reparameterization then turn this reward into a per-category margin loss (Section 3.2). We close with a dual-inspired update rule that adjusts the margins from DPO-internal quantities alone (Section 3.3). Complete proofs and closed-form derivations are provided in Appendix A.

3.1 Per-Category Constraints and the Category-Augmented Reward

Let h⁡(x,y)∈{0,1}h(x,y)\in\{0,1\} be a binary unsafe indicator on response yy to prompt xx, for instance the thresholded cost h=𝟙[c(x,y)>0]h=\mathds{1}[c(x,y)>0] from Section 2.2 or a direct annotation. Index the KK harm categories by 𝒦={1,…,K}\mathcal{K}=\{1,\dots,K\}, and let each prompt xx come with a category set 𝒞⁡(x)⊆𝒦\mathcal{C}(x)\subseteq\mathcal{K} (abbreviated 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} for sample ii) listing the harm types its candidate responses could exhibit. We replace the single global budget of (3) with KK constraints, one per harm category:

maxθ𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼πθ[r(x,y)]−βKL(πθ∥πref)\displaystyle\max_{\theta}\;\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\,y\sim\pi_{\theta}}[r(x,y)]-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}) (4)
s.t.𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼πθ[𝟙[k∈𝒞(x)]h(x,y)]≤ϵk∀k∈𝒦,\displaystyle\text{s.t.}\quad\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\,y\sim\pi_{\theta}}\!\bigl[\mathds{1}[k\in\mathcal{C}(x)]\,h(x,y)\bigr]\leq\epsilon_{k}\quad\forall k\in\mathcal{K},

with per-category tolerances ϵk≥0\epsilon_{k}\geq 0. Each constraint bounds the expected unsafe mass contributed by prompts whose active category set includes kk, under the current policy. Introducing KK dual variables 𝝀=(λ1,…,λK)≥0\bm{\lambda}=(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{K})\geq 0, one per constraint, the Lagrangian of (4) is

ℒ(θ,𝝀)=𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼πθ[r(x,y)−∑k∈𝒞⁡(x)λkh(x,y)]−βKL(πθ∥πref)+∑k=1Kλkϵk,\mathcal{L}(\theta,\bm{\lambda})=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\,y\sim\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[r(x,y)-\!\sum_{k\in\mathcal{C}(x)}\!\lambda_{k}\,h(x,y)\right]-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}})+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\lambda_{k}\epsilon_{k}, (5)

where we have collapsed ∑kλk 1[k∈𝒞(x)]h(x,y)\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}\,\mathds{1}[k\in\mathcal{C}(x)]\,h(x,y) into ∑k∈𝒞⁡(x)λk​h​(x,y)\sum_{k\in\mathcal{C}(x)}\lambda_{k}\,h(x,y) and the final term is constant in θ\theta. Define the category-augmented reward

r𝝀​(x,y)=r⁡(x,y)−∑k∈𝒞⁡(x)λk​h​(x,y),r_{\bm{\lambda}}(x,y)\;=\;r(x,y)\;-\;\sum_{k\in\mathcal{C}(x)}\lambda_{k}\,h(x,y), (6)

which retains the original reward on safe responses (h=0h=0) and penalizes unsafe ones by the sum of multipliers on the prompt’s active categories. At fixed 𝝀\bm{\lambda}, maximizing (5) over θ\theta is equivalent to solving the KL-regularized RL objective with r𝝀r_{\bm{\lambda}} in place of rr:

maxθ𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼πθ[r𝝀(x,y)]−βKL(πθ∥πref).\max_{\theta}\;\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\,y\sim\pi_{\theta}}\!\bigl[r_{\bm{\lambda}}(x,y)\bigr]-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}). (7)

This objective admits a closed-form optimal policy π𝝀∗​(y|x)∝πref​(y|x)​exp⁡(r𝝀​(x,y)/β)\pi^{*}_{\bm{\lambda}}(y|x)\propto\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)\exp(r_{\bm{\lambda}}(x,y)/\beta), and the DPO reparameterization yields a loss of the form (2) on preference pairs.

3.2 Agreement Filtering and the Per-Category Margin Loss

Since r𝝀r_{\bm{\lambda}} combines helpfulness and safety, this loss is well-behaved only on pairs where both signals agree on which response is preferred. SafeDPO (Kim et al., 2026) addresses the special case where the helpfulness-preferred response is unsafe by swapping labels so that the safer response becomes the preferred one. We take a broader approach and discard disagreements. We define 𝒟agree\mathcal{D}_{\text{agree}} as the subset of 𝒟\mathcal{D} restricted to pairs where the helpfulness-preferred response is also safety-preferred.

For a safe-unsafe pair on 𝒟agree\mathcal{D}_{\text{agree}}, h⁡(x,yw)=0h(x,y_{w})=0 and h⁡(x,yl)=1h(x,y_{l})=1; substituting into (6) gives

r𝝀​(x,yw)−r𝝀​(x,yl)=[r⁡(x,yw)−r⁡(x,yl)]+∑k∈𝒞iλk≥r⁡(x,yw)−r⁡(x,yl)> 0,r_{\bm{\lambda}}(x,y_{w})-r_{\bm{\lambda}}(x,y_{l})\;=\;\bigl[r(x,y_{w})-r(x,y_{l})\bigr]+\sum_{k\in\mathcal{C}_{i}}\lambda_{k}\;\geq\;r(x,y_{w})-r(x,y_{l})\;>\;0, (8)

so labels never flip under any 𝝀≥0\bm{\lambda}\geq 0 (Section A.2), and the ∑k∈𝒞iλk\sum_{k\in\mathcal{C}_{i}}\lambda_{k} term acts as an additive margin that the Lagrangian places on safe-unsafe pairs.

However, the sum margin over-penalizes multi-label prompts: a prompt touching multiple categories is not intrinsically more dangerous per category, and the |𝒞i|\lvert\mathcal{C}_{i}\rvert-fold penalty is an artifact of taxonomy granularity rather than intrinsic risk. We instead aggregate by max,

mi​(𝝀)=maxk∈𝒞i⁡λk,m_{i}(\bm{\lambda})\;=\;\max_{k\in\mathcal{C}_{i}}\lambda_{k}, (9)

reading the per-sample margin as the minimum pressure that already satisfies the most-violated category among 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i}. Max aggregation is a deliberate surrogate of the strict Lagrangian (since max≤∑\max\leq\sum); Section A.5 discusses the resulting gap. The Cat-DPO per-sample loss is then

ℒi​(θ,𝝀)={−log⁡σ⁡(β​δi−mi​(𝝀)),safe-unsafe pair,−log⁡σ⁡(β​δi),safe-safe pair.\mathcal{L}_{i}(\theta,\bm{\lambda})\;=\;\begin{cases}-\log\sigma\!\bigl(\beta\delta_{i}-m_{i}(\bm{\lambda})\bigr),&\text{safe-unsafe pair,}\\[1.99997pt] -\log\sigma(\beta\delta_{i}),&\text{safe-safe pair.}\end{cases} (10)

where safe-safe pairs carry no margin because both responses satisfy h=0h=0 and the augmented and original rewards coincide.

To see the mechanism concretely, the gradient of (10) on a safe-unsafe pair is

∇θℒi=−[1−σ⁡(β​δi−mi)]⏟weight​β​∇θδi.\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{i}\;=\;-\,\underbrace{\bigl[1-\sigma(\beta\delta_{i}-m_{i})\bigr]}_{\text{weight}}\;\beta\,\nabla_{\theta}\delta_{i}. (11)

The weight is non-decreasing in mim_{i}, so the margin monotonically raises the gradient threshold. When mi=0m_{i}=0 the weight is large only while the model still prefers the unsafe response; a positive mim_{i} raises this bar to β​δi=mi\beta\delta_{i}=m_{i}, keeping gradient pressure active until the model prefers the safe response by a margin of at least mim_{i}. Once a category is satisfied, λk\lambda_{k} decays toward zero (Section 3.3), the threshold drops, and the gradient relaxes to the standard DPO level. SafeDPO (Kim et al., 2026) raises the threshold uniformly via a fixed Δ\Delta; Cat-DPO adapts it per category through mi=maxk∈𝒞i⁡λkm_{i}=\max_{k\in\mathcal{C}_{i}}\lambda_{k}, concentrating gradient pressure where it is still needed (a detailed comparison is in Section A.3).

3.3 Dual-Inspired Updates and the Training Algorithm

The loss (10) depends on 𝝀\bm{\lambda}, which must be updated during training. In a standard Lagrangian framework, each dual variable is updated by a projected gradient step on the constraint violation: λk←max(0,λk+η(𝔼y∼πθ[𝟙[k∈𝒞(x)]h(x,y)]−ϵ))\lambda_{k}\leftarrow\max(0,\;\lambda_{k}+\eta\,(\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}}[\mathds{1}[k\in\mathcal{C}(x)]\,h(x,y)]-\epsilon)). However, evaluating this expectation requires sampling from the current policy πθ\pi_{\theta}, which DPO’s offline training never does. We instead use a per-sample proxy computed directly from DPO-internal quantities,

Vi≔ 1−σ⁡(β​δi)∈[0,1],V_{i}\;\coloneqq\;1-\sigma(\beta\delta_{i})\;\in\;[0,1], (12)

which is small when the model strongly prefers the safe response on pair ii and close to 11 when it still prefers the unsafe one. For each safe-unsafe sample and every k∈𝒞ik\in\mathcal{C}_{i}, we apply the detached update

λk←max⁡(0,λk+η⁡(Vi−ϵ)),\lambda_{k}\;\leftarrow\;\max\;\!\bigl(0,\,\lambda_{k}+\eta(V_{i}-\epsilon)\bigr), (13)

with dual step size η>0\eta>0. We update every active category in 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i}, not just the arg​max\argmax used in the primal; Section A.5 discusses this choice. The formulation (4) admits a separate tolerance ϵk\epsilon_{k} per category, but we use a single shared ϵ\epsilon so that every category is held to the same safety standard; this reduces the hyperparameter space to two scalars (η,ϵ)(\eta,\epsilon).

By construction, λk\lambda_{k} grows only when Vi>ϵV_{i}>\epsilon (category still unsafe) and decays when Vi<ϵV_{i}<\epsilon (category already safe), approximating the complementary-slackness condition from constrained optimization (Boyd and Vandenberghe, 2004). As a per-sample surrogate, ViV_{i} is directionally correct but biased relative to the population violation. Together with our choice of max-margin primal and per-category dual updates, this makes Cat-DPO a dual-inspired controller rather than an exact primal-dual algorithm. Like Safe-RLHF’s primal-dual (Dai et al., 2024), Cat-DPO uses one-step Arrow–Hurwicz updates (Arrow et al., 1958) rather than exact inner maximization; see Section A.4 for more details. Algorithm 1 summarizes the full procedure.

4 Experiments

We conduct comprehensive experiments to study four questions: (i) does Cat-DPO improve Helpfulness and Harmlessness against baselines (Section 4.1); (ii) does it reduce per-category disparity, and can the reduction be attributed to the category-adaptive margins (Section 4.2); (iii) how sensitive is it to the hyperparameters η\eta and ϵ\epsilon (Section 4.3); (iv) does it maintain safety without introducing over-refusal on an external benchmark (Section 4.4).

Training data. All methods train on the alpaca2-7b subset of PKU-SafeRLHF (Ji et al., 2025). Each entry in the dataset is a tuple (x,y0,y1)(x,y_{0},y_{1}) with two independent binary preference labels for helpfulness and harmlessness, and each unsafe response is annotated with one or more of K=19K{=}19 harm categories. We exclude unsafe-unsafe pairs. More details are in Appendix C. For Cat-DPO and DPO-bettersafe (below), we restrict training to the agreement-filtered subset 𝒟agree\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{agree}} defined in Section 3.2. The other DPO baselines train on the remaining preference pairs with their respective chosen-response labels, and SafeDPO and SACPO apply the pair transformations prescribed in their original formulations.

Backbones and baselines. We train from two reference policies: a reproduced Alpaca-7B SFT model11 1 huggingface.co/PKU-Alignment/alpaca-7b-reproduced-llama-2 (Dai et al., 2024) built on LLaMA-2-7B as the primary backbone, and the Qwen3-4B base checkpoint (Yang et al., 2025a) as a non-safety-primed secondary backbone. On each, we compare Cat-DPO against six baselines: Base, the reference policy without preference training; DPO-helpful and DPO-harmless, standard DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) on the helpfulness and safety preferences respectively; DPO-bettersafe, standard DPO on 𝒟agree\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{agree}}, which shares data with Cat-DPO and differs only in the absence of the per-category margin; SafeDPO (Kim et al., 2026), a fixed-margin direct method that applies a safety margin Δ\Delta to safe-unsafe pairs after a TT-transformation; and SACPO (Wachi et al., 2024), a stepwise helpfulness-then-safety pipeline. SafeDPO and SACPO were developed on the 30K-pair predecessor release of PKU-SafeRLHF; we therefore adopt the authors’ reported best-performing hyperparameters (Δ=10\Delta{=}10 for SafeDPO, β/λ=0.025\beta/\lambda{=}0.025 for SACPO). Detailed training hyperparameters are listed in Appendix C.

Evaluation protocol. We score responses on the test split with two independent judges. Our primary judge is GPT-4o (Hurst et al., 2024) as an LLM-as-a-judge: each prompt is first classified into one of three classes (benign, risky-but-answerable, inherently-harmful), and the response is then scored on a 11–1010 scale for harmlessness and helpfulness using a class-conditional rubric, and safety ratio, the fraction of responses receiving harmlessness strictly above 55; the full classification and scoring prompts are given in Section C.4. The class-conditional design is necessary because the correct behavior depends on intent (Yuan et al., 2025): a flat refusal is the right answer on an inherently harmful prompt but counts as unhelpful on a benign or risky-but-answerable one, and a single uniform rubric conflates these cases. We also report safety ratio under the PKU-SafeRLHF default evaluator released with the dataset, the cost reward model beaver-7b-unified-cost22 2 huggingface.co/PKU-Alignment/beaver-7b-unified-cost, counting a response as safe iff its predicted cost is ≤0\leq 0.

4.1 Main Results

Cat-DPO leads across backbones and judges. Table 1 reports aggregate results on two backbones. On Alpaca-7B, Cat-DPO is the top-trained method on all metrics under both judges. On Qwen3-4B, where all methods approach saturation, Cat-DPO ties or closely trails the best on every metric; the weaker differentiation is expected because Qwen3-4B is a base checkpoint whose output distribution differs from the SFT-generated preference pairs, making the DPO log-ratio less well-specified (Rafailov et al., 2023).

The per-category margin drives the gain. The cleanest single-variable comparison on Alpaca-7B is Cat-DPO against DPO-bettersafe, which trains on the same agreement-filtered data 𝒟agree\mathcal{D}_{\text{agree}} with the same schedule and differs only in the presence of the category-adaptive margin. Cat-DPO leads on every metric, isolating the per-category λk{\lambda_{k}} as the effective ingredient: neither training on 𝒟agree\mathcal{D}_{\text{agree}} without the margin (DPO-bettersafe) nor applying a fixed uniform margin on different data (SafeDPO) recovers these numbers. The choice of 𝒟agree\mathcal{D}_{\text{agree}} itself is validated in Section C.5.

4.2 Per-Category Balance and Its Training-Time Mechanism

Cat-DPO flattens the per-category distribution. Figure 3 reports four summary statistics of the per-category safe ratio distribution over the K=19K{=}19 harm categories under both judges on Alpaca-7B. Cat-DPO is the best method on every panel. The improvement is not a spurious lift of already-easy categories: macro, worst-3, gap, and variance all move in the favorable direction simultaneously, which is only consistent with the hardest categories being genuinely pulled up.

The flattening is driven by the adaptive dual during training. Figure 4 diagnoses the mechanism on Alpaca-7B against the matched DPO-bettersafe run. Three observations form a causal chain. Figure 4(a) shows that λk\lambda_{k} correctly tracks lagging categories: the three hardest carry a persistently higher mean λk\lambda_{k} than the three easiest throughout training. Because a larger λk\lambda_{k} shifts the effective DPO margin (Equation 10), these categories receive stronger gradient pressure. Figure 4(b) confirms the resulting effect: Cat-DPO’s per-category preference probability reaches the saturation ceiling ahead of DPO-bettersafe, and the gap closes only as bettersafe catches up later in training. Figure 4(c) shows that this advantage is not spread uniformly but concentrates on the hardest categories: per-category advantage scales inversely with the category’s preference probability under DPO-bettersafe (Pearson r=−0.70r=-0.70, p<10−3p<10^{-3} over the 1919 categories). Although training-time preference probabilities converge for both methods, the eval-time difference persists because the two runs allocate the finite KL budget differently across categories: the adaptive margin steers more capacity toward hard categories during the critical early phase, improving their generalization on held-out prompts. The net result is the flatter safe ratio distribution in Figure 3.

4.3 Hyperparameter Sensitivity

η\eta has a single peak; ϵ\epsilon traces a helpfulness-safety trade-off. Figure 5(a) shows both Safe Ratio and Helpfulness peak at η=0.5\eta=0.5 on Alpaca-7B and decay on either side. η\eta is the step size in the λk\lambda_{k} update, governing how fast λk\lambda_{k} responds to per-category constraint violations: values below 0.30.3 let λk\lambda_{k} lag the current ViV_{i}, values above 0.50.5 let λk\lambda_{k} overshoot and destabilise training, and η=0.5\eta{=}0.5 is the tracking–stability sweet spot for our training budget. Figure 5(b) shows the two metrics move in opposite directions as ϵ\epsilon varies: smaller ϵ\epsilon drives λk\lambda_{k} up more aggressively and buys extra Safe Ratio at the cost of Helpfulness, while larger ϵ\epsilon relaxes the constraint and preserves more Helpfulness at some safety cost; ϵ=0.02\epsilon{=}0.02 is the Pareto-efficient operating point we use throughout the paper.

We also note that under the default (η,ϵ)=(0.5,0.02)(\eta,\epsilon){=}(0.5,0.02), the cross-category mean λk\lambda_{k} settles at ≈10\approx\!10 during mid training (full per-category trajectories and further discussion in Section C.3), coinciding with the fixed margin Δ=10\Delta{=}10 that SafeDPO adopts as its grid-searched optimum: the two methods independently converge on the same average margin scale from very different search procedures, and Cat-DPO additionally differentiates that average per category.

ϵ\epsilon should match the base model’s capacity. The dual-update rule (13) treats ϵ\epsilon as a target floor for the per-sample proxy Vi=1−σ⁡(β​δi)V_{i}=1-\sigma(\beta\delta_{i}): λk\lambda_{k} stabilises only when the model can drive ViV_{i} below ϵ\epsilon on category kk. A smaller backbone has less capacity to fit the preference pairs, therefore a higher achievable ViV_{i} floor, and should need a larger ϵ\epsilon for λk\lambda_{k} to settle. To test this, we sweep ϵ∈{0.02,0.05,0.07}\epsilon\in\{0.02,0.05,0.07\} on two smaller Qwen3 base checkpoints (Yang et al., 2025a), Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-0.6B. Table 2 confirms the prediction: both metrics peak at ϵ=0.05\epsilon=0.05 rather than at the ϵ=0.02\epsilon=0.02 that is optimal on Alpaca-7B and Qwen3-4B; loosening further to ϵ=0.07\epsilon=0.07 overshoots the floor and degrades both metrics.

4.4 Over-Refusal Evaluation on XSTest

Preference-trained safety alignment can mislead a model into refusing benign prompts that merely share surface cues with unsafe ones, an exaggerated-safety failure mode that (Röttger et al., 2024) introduced XSTest to expose. We use it to check whether Cat-DPO’s per-category margin amplifies this behavior, and whether its safety transfers to a different prompt distribution. The split pairs 250250 superficially risky-sounding benign prompts with 200200 genuinely unsafe prompts. We score each response with a GPT-4o-based LLM-as-a-judge; the full setup is given in Section C.7.

Cat-DPO does not amplify over-refusal on either backbone. On both backbones (Table 3), over-refusal ratio of Cat-DPO stays within 0.4​pp0.4\text{pp} of DPO-harmless, confirming that the per-category margin does not introduce additional over-refusal. On Alpaca-7B, Cat-DPO additionally attains the best safe ratio, refusing more unsafe prompts without over-refusing on benign ones. SafeDPO achieves the lowest over-refusal ratio on Qwen3-4B but also the lowest safe ratio on both backbones, reflecting weaker overall safety training on this backbone rather than better calibration. On Qwen3-4B the safe ratio advantage of Cat-DPO does not carry over, consistent with the distribution mismatch and near-saturation noted in Section 4.1; relaxing ϵ\epsilon or capping λk\lambda_{k} could close this gap.

5 Conclusion

We cast safety alignment as a per-category constrained problem and introduced Cat-DPO, a direct-preference-optimization algorithm that turns each category’s Lagrangian dual variable into an adaptive per-sample margin and updates it from DPO-internal quantities alone. The per-category dual variables automatically identify lagging categories during training and concentrate gradient pressure where safety is still insufficient, producing a flatter per-category distribution without manual tuning.

On Alpaca-7B, Cat-DPO improves aggregate helpfulness and harmlessness, reduces per-category safety disparity, and remains well-calibrated under the XSTest over-refusal benchmark; on Qwen3-4B, where distribution mismatch with the SFT-generated preference data and near-saturation safety limit per-category differentiation, it matches the strongest baselines and leaves room for improvement on XSTest. Beyond method, our results suggest that fine-grained, per-category analysis of safety performance can surface weaknesses that aggregate metrics obscure, and that targeted interventions at the category level can close these gaps without sacrificing overall performance.

For future work, we see three directions. First, the constraint budget ϵ\epsilon currently requires backbone-specific tuning; deriving a default from base-model statistics alone would make the method plug-and-play. Second, the KK harm categories are inherited from the dataset’s annotation scheme rather than chosen; learning the taxonomy end-to-end from pair-level signals, or allowing soft or hierarchical category membership, could capture structure that flat surface labels miss and would extend the method to preference datasets without pre-labeled categories. Third, our dual update is a DPO-internal offline surrogate; combining it with light on-policy corrections or with a capped or regularized λk\lambda_{k} schedule could stabilize the per-category pressure and narrow the gap on already-aligned backbones.

Appendix A Full Derivation of Cat-DPO

We work in the same setting as Section 3: policy πθ\pi_{\theta}, reference model πref\pi_{\text{ref}}, latent helpfulness reward r⁡(x,y)r(x,y), binary unsafe indicator h⁡(x,y)∈{0,1}h(x,y)\in\{0,1\}, category set 𝒞⁡(x)⊆𝒦\mathcal{C}(x)\subseteq\mathcal{K}, per-category constrained problem (4), and category-augmented reward (6).

Closed-form optimal policy. For a fixed dual vector 𝝀≥0\bm{\lambda}\geq 0 and a fixed prompt xx, the inner maximization over the policy conditional π(⋅|x)\pi(\cdot|x) is

a standard KL-regularized RL objective [19, 9]. Let J⁡(π)J(\pi) denote the objective of (14). Expanding the KL term,

J⁡(π)\displaystyle J(\pi) =∑yπ⁡(y|x)​[r𝝀​(x,y)−β​log⁡π⁡(y|x)πref​(y|x)]\displaystyle=\sum_{y}\pi(y|x)\!\left[r_{\bm{\lambda}}(x,y)-\beta\log\!\frac{\pi(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}\right] (15)

J⁡(π)=∑yπ⁡(y|x)​[β​log⁡q⁡(y)−β​log⁡π⁡(y|x)].J(\pi)\;=\;\sum_{y}\pi(y|x)\!\left[\beta\log q(y)-\beta\log\pi(y|x)\right]. (16)

r𝝀​(x,y)=β​log⁡π𝝀∗​(y|x)πref​(y|x)+β​log⁡Z𝝀​(x),r_{\bm{\lambda}}(x,y)\;=\;\beta\log\!\frac{\pi^{*}_{\bm{\lambda}}(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}\;+\;\beta\log Z_{\bm{\lambda}}(x), (20)

which expresses the augmented reward entirely in terms of policy ratios, up to a prompt-dependent constant β​log⁡Z𝝀​(x)\beta\log Z_{\bm{\lambda}}(x). Under the Bradley–Terry model [18], the preference probability for a pair (yw,yl)(y_{w},y_{l}) under r𝝀r_{\bm{\lambda}} is σ⁡(r𝝀​(x,yw)−r𝝀​(x,yl))\sigma\!\bigl(r_{\bm{\lambda}}(x,y_{w})-r_{\bm{\lambda}}(x,y_{l})\bigr), and the β​log⁡Z𝝀​(x)\beta\log Z_{\bm{\lambda}}(x) terms in (20) cancel in the difference between the winner and the loser. Replacing π𝝀∗\pi^{*}_{\bm{\lambda}} by the trainable policy πθ\pi_{\theta} and taking the negative log-likelihood recovers the standard DPO loss (2), with the preference labels (yw,yl)(y_{w},y_{l}) required to be ranked by r𝝀r_{\bm{\lambda}}, not by rr alone. The closed-form π𝝀∗\pi^{*}_{\bm{\lambda}} in (19) ranges over the full policy class, whereas πθ\pi_{\theta} ranges over the parametric family realizable by the learner; the substitution π𝝀∗→πθ\pi^{*}_{\bm{\lambda}}\to\pi_{\theta} therefore inherits the same representation gap implicit in every DPO-family method, and we treat closeness of πθ\pi_{\theta} to π𝝀∗\pi^{*}_{\bm{\lambda}} as an empirical property of expressive language models rather than a quantity we attempt to bound. On the agreement-filtered dataset 𝒟agree\mathcal{D}_{\text{agree}} defined in Section 3.2, this requirement is automatically satisfied for every 𝝀≥0\bm{\lambda}\geq 0, as shown next.

A.2 Agreement Filtering Preserves Label Consistency

𝒟agree\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{agree}} retains only pairs whose helpfulness and safety preferences agree (Section 3.2), which in particular implies h⁡(x,yw)=0h(x,y_{w})=0. For the theoretical argument below we only need the weaker condition h⁡(x,yw)=0h(x,y_{w})=0; the agreement filter is strictly stronger, additionally excluding safe-safe pairs in which the helpfulness winner is the less safe response. To verify label consistency, fix any pair with h⁡(x,yw)=0h(x,y_{w})=0. From (6),

r𝝀​(x,yw)−r𝝀​(x,yl)\displaystyle r_{\bm{\lambda}}(x,y_{w})-r_{\bm{\lambda}}(x,y_{l}) =[r⁡(x,yw)−r⁡(x,yl)]+∑k∈𝒞⁡(x)λk​h​(x,yl)\displaystyle=\;\bigl[r(x,y_{w})-r(x,y_{l})\bigr]+\sum_{k\in\mathcal{C}(x)}\lambda_{k}\,h(x,y_{l}) (21)
≥r⁡(x,yw)−r⁡(x,yl)> 0,\displaystyle\geq\;r(x,y_{w})-r(x,y_{l})\;>\;0,

where the first inequality uses λk≥0\lambda_{k}\geq 0 and h⁡(x,yl)∈{0,1}h(x,y_{l})\in\{0,1\}, and the second is the observed helpfulness preference. For safe-safe pairs the second term vanishes and r𝝀=rr_{\bm{\lambda}}=r; for safe-unsafe pairs it strictly grows the gap. Either way the ordering under r𝝀r_{\bm{\lambda}} matches the ordering under rr, so the DPO loss (2) on 𝒟agree\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{agree}} remains label-consistent at every admissible 𝝀≥0\bm{\lambda}\geq 0, with no preference-swap transformation needed (in contrast to SafeDPO [10]).

A.3 Margin Monotonicity and Comparison with SafeDPO

The monotonicity claim behind (11) follows from a direct calculation. Viewing the surrogate safe-unsafe loss as ϕ⁡(m)=−log⁡σ⁡(s−m)\phi(m)=-\log\sigma(s-m) for fixed s=β​δis=\beta\delta_{i} and m≥0m\geq 0,

ϕ′(m)=−σ′​(s−m)σ⁡(s−m)⋅(−1)=σ⁡(s−m)​(1−σ⁡(s−m))σ⁡(s−m)= 1−σ(s−m)≥ 0,\phi^{\prime}(m)\;=\;-\,\frac{\sigma^{\prime}(s-m)}{\sigma(s-m)}\cdot(-1)\;=\;\frac{\sigma(s-m)\bigl(1-\sigma(s-m)\bigr)}{\sigma(s-m)}\;=\;1-\sigma(s-m)\;\geq\;0, (22)

with equality only in the limit s−m→+∞s-m\to+\infty. For any finite s−ms-m, ϕ′​(m)>0\phi^{\prime}(m)>0 strictly, so a larger per-sample margin yields a strictly larger loss (and correspondingly stronger gradient in θ\theta).

This monotonicity is a statement about optimization dynamics, not about stationary points. It does not imply that adding the margin preserves the optimum of the original constrained problem. SafeDPO’s Proposition 4.4 [10] establishes such a preservation result in the hard-constraint regime c⁡(x,y)≤0c(x,y)\leq 0, applying a fixed Δ\Delta uniformly to all pairs. Cat-DPO operates in a different regime: our finite, category-specific λk\lambda_{k} provide a soft per-category relaxation, and (11) together with (22) characterizes where gradient pressure is directed rather than what the optimum is.

A.4 On the Per-Sample Proxy ViV_{i}

The exact dual ascent direction for constraint kk is governed by the population violation Uk(θ)=𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼πθ(⋅|x)[𝟙[k∈𝒞(x)]h(x,y)]U_{k}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\,y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x)}\!\bigl[\mathds{1}[k\in\mathcal{C}(x)]\,h(x,y)\bigr], which requires sampling from πθ\pi_{\theta}. Our proxy Vi=1−σ⁡(β​δi)V_{i}=1-\sigma(\beta\delta_{i}) is computed entirely from the offline preference pair (xi,yw,i,yl,i)(x_{i},y_{w,i},y_{l,i}) and makes no call to a cost model; we now characterize how it relates to UkU_{k}.

Pairwise directional tracking. On a safe–unsafe pair, the quantity σ⁡(β​δi)\sigma(\beta\delta_{i}) is the probability the model assigns to ordering the safe response above the unsafe one under the Bradley–Terry reparameterization. Low σ⁡(β​δi)\sigma(\beta\delta_{i}) therefore corresponds to failing to discriminate safe from unsafe, and high σ⁡(β​δi)\sigma(\beta\delta_{i}) corresponds to the model already placing most of its mass on the safe response. Taking Vi=1−σ⁡(β​δi)V_{i}=1-\sigma(\beta\delta_{i}) inverts this so that a larger value means a larger per-pair violation: the average of ViV_{i} over a category’s training pairs grows as the model loses on more pairs of that category. In this sense ViV_{i} is a directionally correct per-pair surrogate for the population unsafe rate.

Sources of bias. ViV_{i} is not an unbiased estimator of UkU_{k} for several reasons. (i) The probability σ⁡(β​δi)\sigma(\beta\delta_{i}) is a pairwise quantity that depends on both yw,iy_{w,i} and yl,iy_{l,i}, whereas UkU_{k} is a generative quantity over the unsafe-response distribution induced by πθ\pi_{\theta} at xix_{i}. (ii) The expectation is taken over the fixed offline dataset, not over samples from πθ\pi_{\theta}, so distributional shift during training is not corrected for. (iii) The mapping from log-ratios to probabilities is sigmoid-nonlinear, so 𝔼(x,yw,yl)∼𝒟​[Vi]\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_{w},y_{l})\sim\mathcal{D}}[V_{i}] and 𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼πθ​[h]\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\,y\sim\pi_{\theta}}[h] do not in general coincide even in the limit of a perfectly calibrated model.

Why this suffices in practice. (13) does not require an unbiased estimate of UkU_{k}; it requires a signal whose sign matches the sign of the violation, so that λk\lambda_{k} grows on binding constraints and decays on slack ones. Pairwise directional tracking delivers exactly this: the accumulation in λk\lambda_{k} averages out per-sample noise across the many updates a category receives in an epoch, so that λk\lambda_{k} trends downward on slack constraints and upward on binding ones. What the KKT-style reading of (13) retains is this direction of drift, not the strict complementary-slackness identity λk⋆​(Uk​(θ⋆)−ϵ)=0\lambda_{k}^{\star}\bigl(U_{k}(\theta^{\star})-\epsilon\bigr)=0 at convergence, which would require an unbiased dual signal and is not supported by ViV_{i}. Empirically (Section 4.2) the resulting λk\lambda_{k} trajectories are predictive of per-category improvements, which is the behavioral signature we would expect from a usable surrogate.

Algorithmic regime and scope of the claim. Algorithm 1 is an Arrow–Hurwicz-style one-step primal-dual update [21]: a single SGD step on θ\theta is interleaved with a single projected step on 𝝀\bm{\lambda}, rather than solving maxθ⁡ℒ⁡(θ,𝝀)\max_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta,\bm{\lambda}) to convergence between dual steps. Last-iterate convergence for such updates is available only under convex-concave structure with exact inner maximization, neither of which holds here. In practice, 𝝀\bm{\lambda} evolves on a slower timescale than θ\theta: the dual variables are KK scalars updated by a simple projected step, whereas the primal update moves millions of parameters through a full SGD step, so 𝝀\bm{\lambda} drifts slowly against a fast-adapting θ\theta. This is the two-timescale regime [26] under which one-step primal-dual updates behave as slow-drift dual ascent on a quasi-converged primal, the same empirical regime used in adversarial training, actor-critic methods, and GANs. The empirical λk\lambda_{k} trajectories remain bounded throughout training across all hyperparameter settings reported in Section 4.3, which is consistent with a non-empty feasible set for (4) at our chosen ϵ\epsilon; we do not attempt a formal Slater-type verification.

A.5 Max Aggregation and Primal-Dual Consistency

The strict Lagrangian of (4) yields the sum aggregation misum=∑k∈𝒞iλkm_{i}^{\text{sum}}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{C}_{i}}\lambda_{k}, together with a per-category dual update that evaluates each constraint’s violation against the same primal whose gradient was just taken. Cat-DPO instead uses the max aggregation (9) in the primal and the per-category rule (13) in the dual; the gap between this pairing and the strict Lagrangian is made explicit below.

What the pair (max,per-category)(\text{max},\text{per-category}) is. Strictly speaking, the primal loss (10) under max aggregation is the Lagrangian of a problem whose constraint aggregates categories by max rather than by sum; that is, max-margin is not the Lagrangian of our per-category constraints, and the per-category update (13) is therefore not the primal-dual update of the max-primal objective. The two rules were designed for different constraint structures: the primal handles multi-label samples by charging the most-violated category, while the dual tracks each category’s own violation independently so that a struggling category is not masked by a neighbor that happens to share some of its samples.

Why we still prefer max in the primal. The sum aggregation is primal-dual consistent but charges multi-label samples |𝒞i||\mathcal{C}_{i}| times over for a single gradient step, with no behavioral justification for the over-allocation. A prompt that happens to lie in five categories is not intrinsically five times as dangerous as an otherwise identical prompt in a single category; the multi-label count is an artifact of taxonomy granularity. Max aggregation, by contrast, sizes the per-sample pressure to the most-violated category, namely maxk∈𝒞i⁡λk\max_{k\in\mathcal{C}_{i}}\lambda_{k}. Weaker categories in 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} then receive more pressure than they individually require, which remains feasible since their λk\lambda_{k} is smaller.

Why we still prefer a per-category dual update. The natural alternative to (13) under max primal would be a “binding-category-only” update λk⋆←max⁡(0,λk⋆+η⁡(Vi−ϵ))\lambda_{k^{\star}}\leftarrow\max(0,\lambda_{k^{\star}}+\eta(V_{i}-\epsilon)) with k⋆=arg​maxk∈𝒞i⁡λkk^{\star}=\argmax_{k\in\mathcal{C}_{i}}\lambda_{k}, leaving the other categories in 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} untouched. This is primal-dual consistent with the max primal but introduces a silent ordering effect: a category that happens to share a sample with a temporarily larger λk′\lambda_{k^{\prime}} never sees that sample’s violation signal, even though its own constraint may still be binding. The per-category update (13) gives every category in 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} an independent observation of the sample’s violation, which matches the intuition that each category’s constraint should be tracked independently regardless of the primal aggregator.

Takeaway. The (max, per-category) pairing is a pragmatic compromise: it preserves the per-category bookkeeping that Section 3.3 relies on to reduce inter-category variance, and it avoids the multi-label over-penalty that a strict Lagrangian sum would incur. Cat-DPO is thus best understood as a dual-inspired controller rather than an exact primal-dual method. We do not prove convergence; we rely on the gradient analysis (11)-(22) for the local training-dynamics argument, and on the experiments in Section 4.2 for the empirical connection between λk\lambda_{k} trajectories and per-category improvement.

A.6 Generality of the Per-Category Formulation

The per-category formulation (4) strictly generalizes the single-budget constraint of Safe RLHF [7], and the shared tolerance ϵ\epsilon used in Section 3.3 is a deliberate simplification rather than a limitation.

Reduction to the single-budget form. Setting K=1K=1 and 𝒞⁡(x)≡{1}\mathcal{C}(x)\equiv\{1\} collapses the category indicator in (4) to 𝟙[1∈𝒞(x)]≡1\mathds{1}[1\in\mathcal{C}(x)]\equiv 1, so the constraint reduces to 𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼πθ​[h⁡(x,y)]≤ϵ1\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\,y\sim\pi_{\theta}}[h(x,y)]\leq\epsilon_{1}. Choosing ϵ1=d\epsilon_{1}=d and instantiating hh as the binarization h=𝟙[c>0]h=\mathds{1}[c>0] of the Safe RLHF cost then recovers (3) exactly. Any result that held for a global cost budget is therefore a special case of the per-category analysis in Sections A.1, A.2 and A.3.

Shared versus per-category tolerances. Our experiments use a shared tolerance ϵk≡ϵ\epsilon_{k}\equiv\epsilon, which turns the constraint budget into a single scalar hyperparameter and is the value referenced by the dual update (13). The formulation itself admits arbitrary {ϵk}\{\epsilon_{k}\} at no algorithmic cost: an operator wishing to encode differential risk budgets (e.g., a stricter bar on illegal content than on mildly off-topic responses) can substitute per-category ϵk\epsilon_{k} directly into both the primal constraint and the dual update, and the derivations of Sections A.1, A.2, A.3, A.4 and A.5 go through unchanged. We leave an empirical study of non-uniform ϵk\epsilon_{k} for future work.

Appendix B Related Work

Cat-DPO sits at the intersection of three lines of work: preference-based alignment of LLMs, safety-aware direct alignment, and constrained optimization with worst-case robustness.

B.1 Preference-Based Alignment of LLMs

RLHF [8, 1] introduced the reward-model-then-PPO pipeline that underlies most aligned language models, and DPO [9, 27] recast the same objective as a classification-style loss on preference pairs, eliminating the reward model. A number of follow-up variants modify the loss form (IPO [28], KTO [29], SimPO [30]) while inheriting DPO’s single-scalar optimization structure. A separate line introduces sample-adaptive margins into DPO: α\alpha-DPO [31] derives per-pair margins from the balance between the policy and the reference distribution; MADPO [32] trains an auxiliary reward model to estimate per-pair margin magnitudes; and AMaPO [33] adds instance-wise margins via zz-normalized scoring. Cat-DPO shares the adaptive-margin motif with these methods but operates at a different granularity: all three assign margins per pair from pair-specific features, whereas we assign margins per category and derive them from an explicit Lagrangian dual, making Cat-DPO orthogonal to and in principle composable with any of them. Safe RLHF [7] was the first to cast safety alignment as an explicit constrained problem, adding a cost model alongside the reward model and solving it with PPO-Lagrangian; it is the direct conceptual ancestor of our formulation.

B.2 Safety-Aware Direct Alignment

Our closest prior work is SafeDPO [10], which folds a hard safety constraint into a tractable DPO-style loss with a fixed margin Δ\Delta and proves equivalence to the constrained optimum under its assumptions. SACPO [11] decomposes safety alignment into two sequential DPO stages, first on helpfulness preferences and then on safety preferences, as a stepwise alternative to the fused-loss approach. Both methods use a single global safety signal (a fixed margin or a sequential stage) applied identically to every training pair regardless of which harm category the pair touches. Cat-DPO’s distinguishing move is to replace that single signal with KK per-category adaptive margins, derived from the Lagrangian of a per-category constrained problem and updated online during training.

B.3 Constrained Optimization and Worst-Case Robustness

The theoretical machinery we use (Lagrangian relaxation, dual ascent, complementary slackness) is standard in Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs) [34]. [35] established zero duality gap for CMDPs, and [36] gave a natural-policy-gradient primal-dual algorithm with convergence guarantees; in the alignment context, [37] explore closed-form dual solutions for single-constraint safety. Cat-DPO adapts this machinery to the offline DPO regime, where the essential change is the proxy Vi=1−σ⁡(β​δi)V_{i}=1-\sigma(\beta\delta_{i}) that replaces on-policy rollouts as the feedback signal for dual updates.

A complementary line treats the imbalance problem through worst-case optimization. Group DRO [12] minimizes worst-group loss via exponentiated-gradient updates on group weights, and several recent works transport this idea into preference learning. GRPO [13] embeds group information in the prompt context and optimizes a minimax worst-group objective in reward-free RLHF; Dr. DPO [14] adds pairwise distributional robustness to the DPO loss; WDPO and KLDPO [15] use Wasserstein and KL-ball distributionally-robust formulations; and EM-DPO [16] handles unobserved preference heterogeneity through a minimax regret over latent subgroups. Cat-DPO differs from this line in mechanism: our per-category margins are Lagrangian dual variables of explicit per-category constraints, not weights from a minimax or distributionally-robust objective.

Finally, MODPO [38] extends DPO to multiple competing reward objectives via separate reward heads; our setting is distinct, with a single safety objective decomposed into KK sub-distributions each carrying its own constraint rather than KK competing objectives to balance.

Appendix C Experimental Details

C.1 Dataset Details

All experiments use the alpaca2-7b subset of PKU-SafeRLHF [17]. The raw subset contains 25,56425{,}564 training and 2,8482{,}848 test preference entries. Each entry is a tuple (x,y0,y1)(x,y_{0},y_{1}) with two independent binary preference labels (helpfulness and harmlessness), and each unsafe response is annotated with one or more of K=19K{=}19 harm categories. Table 4 lists all 1919 categories with their definitions (reproduced from [17]) and training-set frequency under the agreement filter.

Training-set filtering. All methods exclude unsafe-unsafe pairs (11,01911{,}019 entries), leaving 14,54514{,}545 preference pairs. Cat-DPO and DPO-bettersafe additionally require the helpfulness and safety preferences to agree (Section 3.2), yielding 11,77111{,}771 training pairs; the other DPO baselines train on the full 14,54514{,}545. SafeDPO applies its own pair-swap transformation on the 14,54514{,}545 pairs.

Test-set processing. For evaluation, we deduplicate prompts and retain only those for which at least one of the two responses carries a harm-category annotation, yielding 1,6201{,}620 unique test prompts. The per-category evaluation in Section 4.2 requires assigning each prompt a category set 𝒞⁡(x)\mathcal{C}(x). Because PKU-SafeRLHF annotates categories at the response level rather than the prompt level, we use the union of both responses’ category annotations as a proxy for 𝒞⁡(x)\mathcal{C}(x): a prompt is considered to touch category kk if either of its two dataset responses is labeled with kk. This is a conservative proxy that may over-assign categories to a prompt, but it ensures that every category relevant to the prompt’s risk profile is represented. To verify that this filtering does not bias the aggregate results, we also evaluate on the full deduplicated test set (2,7742{,}774 prompts, including the 1,1541{,}154 safe-safe prompts excluded from Table 1). Table 5 reports the same metrics as Table 1 on this expanded set; the ranking of all methods is identical, confirming that the filtered evaluation is representative.

Category coupling. Per-category treatment is useful only if the categories carry distinct information; if all categories were perfectly correlated, the KK dual variables would collapse to a single effective scalar and Cat-DPO would reduce to a fixed-margin method. The 1919 PKU-SafeRLHF categories are multi-label but largely independent. [17] present a pairwise correlation analysis (their Figure 4) indicating that most category pairs exhibit low or negative correlation.

C.2 Training Parameters

Experiments are conducted on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q Workstation Edition. All methods share the optimizer and schedule settings in Table 6; method-specific hyperparameters (Δ\Delta for SafeDPO, β/λ\beta/\lambda for SACPO, (η,ϵ)(\eta,\epsilon) for Cat-DPO) are fixed at the values reported in Table 1. For Cat-DPO, we initialize every dual variable at λk=0\lambda_{k}{=}0 and detach the dual update in (13) from the primal graph, so that the primal DPO gradient is computed with the current {λk}\{\lambda_{k}\} treated as constants and each batch then updates the λk\lambda_{k} values once using the per-sample proxy ViV_{i} on the same batch.

C.3 Per-Category Dual-Variable Trajectories

Two features of Figure 6 are worth noting. First, the cross-category mean λk\lambda_{k} stabilizes near 1010 from mid training onward and the per-category values spread over roughly [3,23][3,23]; this spread is the training-time footprint of the adaptive margin that drives the distribution flattening in Section 4.2. Second, a subset of categories (Privacy, Insulting Behavior, Discriminatory Behavior, Cybercrime) ends training with λk\lambda_{k} still in the 1515–2323 range, well above the cross-category mean, and showing no sign of the monotone decay toward zero that Arrow-Hurwicz primal-dual updates [21] would produce at an exact KKT point. Two factors contribute, neither of which is a pathology of Cat-DPO. (i) Our dual update is a DPO-internal surrogate (Equation 12–Equation 13) applied on an offline batch, not the on-policy Arrow-Hurwicz update whose convergence guarantees are stated under population expectations (Section A.4 discusses the bias of ViV_{i}); the empirical λk\lambda_{k} trajectory need not reach a fixed point within a DPO training budget. (ii) Even at an exact fixed point, λk\lambda_{k} would decay only for categories on which the model satisfies 𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼πθ[h(x,y) 1[k∈𝒞(x)]]≤ϵk\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\,y\sim\pi_{\theta}}[h(x,y)\,\mathds{1}[k\in\mathcal{C}(x)]]\leq\epsilon_{k}; categories where the model cannot reach this floor, either because of intrinsic difficulty or because of limited capacity, would keep λk\lambda_{k} active. This is exactly the model-scale pattern observed in Table 2: small backbones cannot reach ϵ=0.02\epsilon{=}0.02 on the hardest categories, and relaxing ϵ\epsilon lets their λk\lambda_{k} settle. We therefore view the persistently high λk\lambda_{k} on the lagging categories as informative rather than undesirable: they flag the categories on which the model’s helpfulness–safety frontier is still binding when training stops, and they are consistent with our choice to stop at a fixed DPO budget rather than run to convergence.

C.4 LLM-as-a-Judge Prompts

Our GPT-4o evaluation (Table 1) applies one classification call and one scoring call per test response. The classification call receives the prompt only and returns one of three labels; the scoring call receives the prompt and the response and returns integer harmlessness and helpfulness scores on a 11–1010 scale using the rubric that matches the predicted class. All prompt templates are listed below.

The classifier receives a system prompt and a user message.

In both the classification and scoring calls the model is queried with temperature 00 and a single completion; responses that fail JSON parsing (fewer than 0.1%0.1\% across our runs) are re-queried up to three times before being dropped from the averages.

Judge robustness. To verify that our findings are not an artifact of the particular judge model, we re-evaluate all methods with GPT-4.1-mini [39] using the same prompts and rubrics (Table 7). The method ranking is preserved, with Cat-DPO leading on all three metrics. The absolute scores differ from GPT-4o: Safe Ratio is uniformly higher while Helpfulness and Harmlessness means are slightly lower. Inspecting the per-response score distributions reveals the cause: GPT-4.1-mini rarely assigns borderline scores in the 44–66 range, instead polarizing toward 11–33 or 77–1010. This polarization inflates the binary Safe Ratio (which thresholds at >5>5) while compressing the mean. Since the ranking is stable across judges and the absolute differences reflect judge calibration rather than method behavior, we adopt GPT-4o as the primary judge throughout the paper.

C.5 Data-Mode Ablation

Cat-DPO trains on the agreement-filtered subset 𝒟agree\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{agree}} (Section 3.2), which retains only pairs where the helpfulness-preferred response is also the safer one. Two natural alternatives exist: (1) applying SafeDPO’s pair-swap transformation [10], which keeps all safe-unsafe pairs but swaps the label when the helpful-preferred response is unsafe; and (2) relaxing the agreement filter to include safe-safe disagree pairs (where both responses are safe but the helpfulness and safety preferences point in opposite directions). We evaluate both alternatives on Alpaca-7B using the reward-model judge.

Agreement filter vs. pair-swap. Table 8 compares the two data-processing strategies, each at its own best hyperparameters. Cat-DPO on 𝒟agree\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{agree}} outperforms Cat-DPO on the SafeDPO-transformed data on every metric despite using fewer training pairs, and Cat-DPO on SafeDPO-transformed data also under-performs SafeDPO itself. The root cause is a training-signal conflict. On 𝒟agree\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{agree}}, every pair’s chosen response is both more helpful and safer, so the primal receives a consistent signal in which helpfulness and safety are aligned. The SafeDPO-transformed data mixes in two types of disagreement pairs: safe-safe pairs where the chosen response is more helpful but less safe (2,4112{,}411 pairs), and label-swapped safe-unsafe pairs where the chosen response is safer but less helpful (363363 pairs). These conflicting pairs destabilize the primal, making ViV_{i} a noisier proxy: some categories quickly reach Vi<ϵV_{i}<\epsilon (so λk→0\lambda_{k}\to 0), while others are disproportionately affected by the conflicting pairs and maintain high ViV_{i} (so λk\lambda_{k} stays elevated). The result is a polarized λk\lambda_{k} distribution: at the end of training on SafeDPO-transformed data, 99 of 1919 categories have λk<0.1\lambda_{k}<0.1 while the rest span up to 17.817.8, compared to 𝒟agree\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{agree}} where all 1919 categories remain active (λk>0.5\lambda_{k}>0.5) with a smooth spread of [3,23][3,23]. SafeDPO’s fixed Δ\Delta is unaffected because it does not adapt to per-sample signals, so the training-signal conflict does not propagate into the margin.

Strict vs. relaxed agreement filter. Table 9 isolates the effect of the safe-safe disagree pairs alone, with both runs at matched (η,ϵ)=(0.5,0.05)(\eta,\epsilon){=}(0.5,0.05). Adding the 2,4112{,}411 safe-safe disagree pairs degrades performance even more than the SafeDPO pair-swap, confirming that these pairs are the primary source of signal conflict: they train the primal to prefer helpful responses even when they are less safe, directly undermining the safety alignment that Cat-DPO relies on.

Both comparisons support the same conclusion: Cat-DPO’s adaptive margin benefits from a clean training signal where helpfulness and safety preferences align, which the agreement filter provides.

C.6 Qualitative Example

Table 10 shows a representative case from the Insulting Behavior category, which has the highest final λk\lambda_{k} (23.523.5) under Cat-DPO and the largest per-category advantage over baselines. Cat-DPO clearly refuses the request and redirects toward positive framing, while DPO-harmless provides a veiled insult template and SafeDPO gives an ambiguous response that the LLM judge still classifies as unsafe. The LLM-as-a-judge scores confirm the distinction: Cat-DPO receives Harmlessness 1010 while both baselines score ≤5\leq 5.

C.7 XSTest Evaluation Details

We evaluate on the contrast split of XSTest [25] using the authors’ public prompt release33 3 github.com/paul-rottger/xstest, specifically the xstest_v2_prompts.csv file, which is a refined prompt set released by the authors after the original conference publication. The split contains 250250 safe-contrast prompts paired with 200200 unsafe-contrast variants that share surface cues with the safe ones. Each generated response is classified into full-compliance, full-refusal, or partial-refusal following the rubric of Röttger et al. [25]; we reuse the authors’ classification prompt template verbatim and use GPT-4o as the judge.

Following [10], we report two metrics. Over-Refusal Ratio is the fraction of the 250250 safe-contrast prompts classified into full-refusal or partial-refusal. Safe Ratio is the corresponding combined partial-plus-full refusal fraction on the 200200 unsafe-contrast prompts.

Appendix D Limitations

The dual update is a DPO-internal offline surrogate rather than an on-policy primal-dual iteration, so convergence guarantees from the classical constrained-optimization literature do not directly apply (Section C.3). The constraint budget ϵ\epsilon must be tuned per backbone (Sections 4.3 and 4.4) and is not automatically set. Training is restricted to the agreement-filtered subset 𝒟agree\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{agree}} (Section 3.2), which discards pairs where the helpfulness-preferred response is the less safe one.

Appendix E Broader Impact

Cat-DPO targets per-category safety disparity in preference-trained language models: if deployed, it could improve safety coverage on harm categories that current uniform-scalar methods underserve. The method does not introduce new capability for generating unsafe content; it operates on existing preference datasets and modifies only the training loss. We see no significant risk of misuse beyond those already present in the underlying DPO framework.

During the preparation of this manuscript, LLM-based tools were used to assist with writing, grammar correction, preliminary data cleaning, and figure and plot design.
